sections.overview: The Cuban fruit-eating bat is a medium-sized phyllostomid of the Greater Antilles, found on Cuba, Hispaniola, Grand Cayman and Middle Caicos; fossil remains are known from Jamaica.
sections.identification: Its short, pig-like muzzle and reduced noseleaf help distinguish it from the sympatric Cuban flower bat Phyllonycteris poeyi, which has a conspicuous uropatagial spur.
sections.habitat: It roosts in caves; in Cuba it often occupies deep, warm and humid chambers, while in Middle Caicos it uses a wider range of cooler caves where deep caverns are scarce.
sections.diet: It is an omnivorous flower visitor whose diet includes pollen, nectar, fruits, seeds and insects. A Cuban study found that flower-visiting bat species partition floral resources, with diets and visitation rates differing among species.
sections.behavior: It forms cave-roosting colonies and uses echolocation when flying; research on Cuban colonies has also documented social distress calls and responses to them.
sections.reproduction: Females form maternity groups and usually give birth to one young; reported birth periods extend across winter and spring, although timing varies among islands.
sections.ecology: It shares its genus with the larger B. cavernarum, found from Puerto Rico through the Lesser Antilles; within Cuban cave communities it overlaps with nectar-feeding relatives such as Phyllonycteris poeyi but differs in diet breadth.
sections.conservation: Mammal Diversity Database and the Cuban species account report Least Concern; cave disturbance and colony counts nevertheless deserve monitoring because many individuals can depend on a small number of roosts.
